column3: Directly parallels fearing the Merciful unseen and adds the returning heart as the recipient's inward response.
Adds the promised outcome for a returning, vigilant person after the preceding inward-response parallel.
Directly supplies forgiveness and great reward as God's promise to believing, righteous responders.
Closely restates warning reaching those who fear their Lord unseen, while adding prayer and personal accountability.
Identifies the Quran as wise, grounding the reminder that the receptive person follows.
Defines the revealed reminder as something explained to people, clarifying the object of following.
Nearly restates fear of the Lord unseen joined to forgiveness and a great reward.
Establishes the addressee as a messenger, supplying the speaker behind the warning in the focus ayah.
Shows dhikr as a selectively related account, adding a narrative use of the reminder.
Generic forgiveness and reward for patient righteous people adds little after the earlier direct promise.
Locates the surrounding message in a descent from the Mighty, Merciful source.
Parallels forgiveness and generous provision for believers who act rightly, though less directly than 5:9.
Frames warning as effective for one who fears, complementing the focus's selective audience.
Restates the messenger's warning role but adds little beyond the immediately preceding focus context.
Adds an eschatological form of good news for believers without the focus's unseen fear or reminder.
Its noble reward for lending to God does not clarify the warning, following, or mercy in the focus ayah.
The immediately preceding contrast explains why warning benefits only a receptive follower.
Pairs divine instruction with giving good news to believers, extending the focus's command to announce glad tidings.
Its general forgiveness and reward formula is redundant with stronger earlier reward parallels.
Places the messenger on a straight path, supplying the route associated with the revealed warning.
Offers another believer's forgiveness and noble provision formula, largely redundant with earlier examples.
Connects the Merciful, the unseen, and a fulfilled promised garden, extending the focus's future good news.
States the local purpose of warning a heedless people, directly setting up the focus's selective efficacy.
Links reminder with a receptive, retaining ear, clarifying the hearing and uptake implied by following dhikr.
Provides the contrary case: hearing recited signs yet persisting arrogantly leads to punitive rather than joyful tidings.
Presents the Quran's descent and humane purpose, adding context for revelation as reminder.
Combines the messenger's warning and good news with a limit on human knowledge of the unseen.
Adds a second contrary response to recited signs: turning away as though one had not heard.
Begins the nearby messenger parable that concretizes reception and rejection of warning.
Explicitly commands following what was sent down and contrasts it with following other patrons.
Restates fearing the Lord unseen while adding anxious awareness of the Hour.
Shows hostile rejection within the adjacent messenger parable, but adds less than the main framing verses.
Calls people to believe and follow the messenger, extending the focus's following into communal guidance.
Its forgiveness and reward for etiquette before the messenger is too generic after earlier reward parallels.
Names revelation a reminder for one who fears, closely complementing the focus's dhikr and fear.
A generic believer reward formula is redundant with stronger earlier formulations.
The mention of male and female does not develop warning, following, unseen fear, or promised reward.
Continues the local account of messengers sent and denied, illustrating the focus's warning setting.
Joins a command sent down with God-consciousness, expiation, and enlarged reward.
Contrasts following truth with turning away from one's reminder, sharpening the significance of following dhikr.
Shows the favorable end of the parable's believing respondent, extending the focus's promised good news.
Reserves knowledge of the unseen to God, supplying a boundary for the focus's unseen orientation.
The mention of male and female has no focused contribution to the ayah's warning-response pattern.
Adds a reward for good conduct but is a distant and redundant instance of recompense.
Being absent from punishment does not clarify fear of the unseen or the receptive response to warning.
Provides a contrary model of following desire without knowledge, weaker than the direct command to follow revelation.
Records the parable's denial that the Merciful sent anything, directly contrasting with the revealed warning.
Frames an unseen narrative as revelation to the messenger, supporting the link between revelation and hidden knowledge.
The creation of sexual pairs does not add to the focus ayah.
The description of people in the Garden does not clarify the focus's warning or response.
Names God knower of unseen and visible and Merciful, but does not add the warning-response relation.
The denial of pleasantness or nobility in punishment is only a lexical overlap with generous reward.
Shows revelation giving a future report while its subjects are unaware, adding a concrete hidden-knowledge disclosure.
Questions a person's claim to knowledge of the unseen, marking a boundary against unauthorized certainty.
A noble station in an abandoned land does not illuminate the focus's reward or warning.
Continues the local messengers' assertion of their commission, reinforcing the source of the warning.
Its enduring reward for believers is too general to add after the earlier reward material.
Connects fear of God with knowledge and forgiveness, adding a distinct profile of reverent response.
The sign of carrying descendants in a ship is not tied to the focus ayah's warning-response theme.
Its broad forgiveness and garden reward formula is redundant with stronger earlier candidates.
Identifies the Quran as possessing dhikr, reinforcing the reminder that the focus describes as followed.
Makes a past event an admonition for one who fears, but adds little beyond closer fear-and-reminder parallels.
Returns deeds to the Knower of unseen and visible without clarifying reception of the reminder.
Records rejection of a reminder being singled out to a messenger, a useful contrast to accepting dhikr.
Defines the messengers' duty as clear delivery, directly completing the warning role in the focus context.
Places every hidden matter in a clear book, adding a record-based frame for the unseen.
Combines the Merciful with an explicit command to follow and obey a messenger's instruction.
The creation of other conveyances does not add to the warning, following, or promised reward.
Its land and gratitude scene does not clarify the focus, and the forgiveness overlap is only contrast evidence.
Calls the Quran noble but adds only a loose characterization after stronger reminder and revelation parallels.
Shows the parable's warning being treated as an unwelcome reminder, providing an immediate rejection contrast.
Completes the believing man's outcome with his Lord's forgiveness and honored status.
The refutation of divine sonship does not develop the focus ayah's warning-response relation.
The command separating wrongdoers is not connected closely enough to the focus's receptive audience.
Commands reminding where it benefits, directly reinforcing the focus's selective efficacy of warning.
Commands the messenger to follow what was revealed, extending following into obedience to revelation.
States that every town could have a warner, but adds little after the local messenger and warning passages.
Invokes forgiveness and mercy in supplication without the focus's recipient, warning, or future-reward pattern.
Portrays refusal to respond as following desire without guidance, a secondary contrary reading of following.
Shows the believing speaker's worshipful orientation to the Creator and return to Him within the local parable.
Mentions believers who follow the Prophet, but supplies little about reminder, fear, or good news.
Limits knowledge to God while defining the messenger as a clear warner.
The sudden incapacity to make a bequest or return home does not clarify the focus ayah.
Distinguishes prophetic service from seeking human payment, a limited contrast to God's promised reward.
Directly commands following what is revealed from the Lord, though it is less audience-specific than 7:3.
The speaker's rejection of other gods does not materially clarify the focus's warning-response pattern.
The cosmic cycle and forgiving divine name do not add to the focus, and the route is contrast-only.
Answers demands for signs by limiting the messenger to clear warning, clarifying the warning role's scope.
The ordered motion of celestial bodies is unrelated to the focus ayah's receptive warning.
Challenges people claiming possession of unseen knowledge, adding a boundary to the unseen theme.
The account of rain, fruits, and mountains does not add to the focus ayah.
Gives the parable's direct call to follow unpaid, rightly guided messengers, concretizing following dhikr.
Links sent prophets as bearers of good news and warning with a revealed book for human disagreement.
Names a warning for humankind but adds little beyond closer descriptions of the messenger's warning.
Inheritance rules do not develop warning, reminder, unseen fear, or promised reward.
Combines the message as a reminder for all worlds with refusal to seek payment for it.
The change of prayer direction does not clarify the focus ayah's warning-response pattern.
Generic repentance, forgiveness, and mercy add little after the direct forgiveness-and-reward parallels.
The creation argument and rain scene do not contribute to the focus ayah.
The townspeople's excitement is only a lexical overlap with good news and gives no focused link.
Explains the immediate limiting case: many are already bound by a decisive word and therefore do not believe.
Depicts the inner constraint that makes the preceding unreceptiveness to warning concrete.
Adds the surrounding image of barriers and obscured sight that explains failure to receive guidance.
Introduces the believing man who runs from the city to urge his people toward the messengers.
Makes the parable's believer reject rival gods, showing the alternative to refusing the messengers' warning.
States the believing man's explicit faith in the people's Lord and his call for them to hear it.
Nearly states the focus's selective warning principle: only those who fear their Lord unseen can be warned.
Places the messenger in the recurring history of warners sent to communities.
Links reciting God's Book, prayer, and spending to hoped-for divine recompense.
Completes that Book-recitation response with full payment of wages and added divine bounty.
Describes the Book as guidance for the God-conscious, clarifying the receptive audience of the reminder.
Names the Quran as confirmation, guidance, and good news for believers.
Defines the messenger as sent with truth to bear good news and warning.
Calls revelation a clarification, guidance, and admonition for the God-conscious.
Frames messengers as bearers of good news and warners so people have no excuse before God.
Shows the messenger explaining from the Book, expanding the function of revealed reminder.
Explicitly denies that people can claim no bearer of good news or warner came to them.
Commands the messenger to convey what was revealed from his Lord.
States that the Quran was revealed so the messenger may warn those whom it reaches.
Directs warning toward those who fear being gathered to their Lord.
Calls the Quran a reminder for all worlds rather than a message purchased from its recipients.
Commands following the blessed Book and God-consciousness so that mercy may be received.
Identifies the revealed Book as warning for people and reminder for believers.
Connects belief with the messenger's command to give believers good news of their standing with their Lord.
Describes the revealed message as admonition, healing, guidance, and mercy for believers.
Presents prophetic narrative as lesson, confirmation, detailed guidance, and mercy for believers.
Characterizes the Book as bringing people from darkness into light by their Lord's permission.
Calls revelation a proclamation through which people are warned, understand divine unity, and remember.
Identifies God as sender and guardian of the dhikr itself.
Defines the messenger as a clear warner.
Describes revelation sent with the command to warn of God's sole divinity and fear Him.
Characterizes the Book as explanation, guidance, mercy, and good news for those who submit.
Links the Quran's straightest guidance to good news of a great reward for believing righteous people.
Names the Quran healing and mercy for believers, extending the focus's merciful result of receptivity.
Pairs the Quran's descent in truth with the messenger's role as bearer of good news and warner.
States that the upright Book warns of severe punishment and gives believers good news of a good reward.
Commands reciting what has been revealed from the Lord's Book.
Makes the Quran easy in the messenger's tongue to give good news to the God-conscious and warn disputers.
Links worship and established prayer to God's remembrance.
Describes the Quranic account as a reminder given from God.
Sets out the burden borne by one who turns away from God's reminder.
Calls the Quran an Arabic warning containing varied warnings so people may become God-conscious or remember.
Provides the direct contrary outcome for one who turns away from God's reminder.
States that the messenger warns by revelation and that the deaf do not hear warning when warned.
Calls the Quran a blessed reminder sent down by God.
Defines the messenger as a clear warner.
Questions whether people have failed to reflect on the word that came to them.
States that the messenger calls people to a straight path.
Names sent verses, an example, and admonition for the God-conscious.
Describes the Criterion's descent so its messenger may be a warner to all worlds.
Explains the Quran's staged sending as a means to strengthen the messenger's heart.
Places the trustworthy Spirit's descent upon the messenger's heart so that he may be among the warners.
Names the Quran guidance and good news for believers.
Describes the Book as insight, guidance, and mercy so people may remember.
States that God's word was brought successively to people so that they may remember.
Commands reciting the revealed Book and pairs it with prayer, an enacted response to revelation.
Calls the Book recited to people sufficient, mercy, and a reminder for believers.
Presents the Book as a truthful revelation intended to warn a previously unwarned people.
Names the Prophet a witness, bearer of good news, and warner.
Describes the messenger's mission to all people as bearer of good news and warner.
Describes the sent Book as discourse that moves those who fear their Lord and then brings them to God's remembrance.
Links God's revealed command to the instruction to warn of the Day of Meeting.
Defines the Quranic messenger as bearer of good news and warner, while noting that many turn away.
Supplies the hostile contrary response: people urge one another not to listen to this Quran.
Calls the Quran guidance and healing for believers while describing unbelievers as deaf to it.
States that an Arabic Quran was revealed to warn the central city and those around it of the Gathering Day.
Limits the messenger's responsibility to clear conveyance when people turn away.
Questions whether the reminder should be withheld because its audience is transgressive.
Shows turning away from the Merciful's reminder leading to a persistently accompanying tempter.
Calls the Quran a reminder for the messenger and his people, for which they will be questioned.
Describes the Quran as made easy in the messenger's tongue so people may remember.
Pairs an earlier guiding, merciful Book with an Arabic confirming Book that warns wrongdoers and gives good news to those who do good.
Commands reminding by the Quran whoever fears God's warning.
States that reminding benefits believers.
Declares the Quran made easy for remembrance and asks whether anyone will remember.
Links messengers and the sent Book with a public standard of justice, broadening revelation's operative purpose.
Describes the messenger reciting verses, purifying, and teaching the Book and wisdom to an unlearned people.
States that God sent down a reminder for those of understanding who believe.
Identifies that reminder as a messenger reciting clear verses to bring believers from darkness into light.
Calls the Quran a reminder for the God-conscious.
Describes the heard Quran as guiding to right conduct and prompting faith in it.
Names the revelation a reminder through which one may choose a path to the Lord.
Calls the passage a reminder and connects willing response to taking a path to God.
Defines the Quran as nothing but a reminder for all worlds.
Describes a messenger from God reciting purified scriptures.
